title: Printing and variables
subtitle: Revise 360 Python course  |  Beyond the OCR J277 specification
intro: Every program you will ever write starts here: putting something on the screen, keeping a value under a name and asking the user for one. Work through the six stations and you will have written your first real programs.
objectives: know how to print lines of output in the order a task asks for
know how to hold a value in a variable or a constant, and how to read one with input()
understand why a value that has been typed in must be cast before it can be calculated with
starter: Three lines run in this order: a = 40, then a = 65, then print(a). Write down exactly what is printed, and explain in one sentence what became of the first value.
keyq: Why must a program decide the data type of a value before it can do anything useful with it?

stations.name: Printing output
bullets: print() puts one value on the screen and then moves down to the next line.
Text to be shown exactly as written goes inside quotation marks, and one print() gives one line of output.
Common mistake: leaving the quotation marks off, so Python hunts for a variable with that name instead.
stations.challenge: Why does Python treat ready and "ready" as two completely different things?
stations.fact: Each print() shows one value and then moves on to...

stations.name: Variables
bullets: A variable is a named box in memory holding one value, and the name always goes on the left of the equals sign.
A constant is a value the program never changes once it is set, and its name is written in capitals.
Common mistake: a second assignment replaces the value, it does not add to it.
stations.challenge: What becomes of the first value when the same variable is given a second one?
stations.fact: In programming = means 'put this in here', so a second assignment does not add to the value, it...

stations.name: Reading input
bullets: input() stops the program, waits for a line to be typed and hands that line back.
Store what comes back in a variable, or the value the user typed is thrown away.
Common mistake: reading two answers into the same variable, so the first one is lost.
stations.challenge: Why can a program print its answers in a different order from the one it asked the questions in?
stations.fact: input() is patient: a program will sit on that line until...

stations.name: Numbers and text
bullets: Integers count whole things, floats hold decimals, strings hold text and booleans hold True or False.
+ adds two numbers but joins two strings end to end, so the data type decides what + means.
Common mistake: joining a number to a string with +, which Python refuses to do.
stations.challenge: Which data type would you choose for a value of 1.50, and why?
stations.fact: Joining two strings end to end has its own name:...

stations.name: Casting
bullets: Casting changes a value from one data type into another.
int() and float() turn text into a number, and str() turns a number into text.
Common mistake: adding to what input() handed back without casting it first, which joins the digits on the end instead.
stations.challenge: Why does int(input()) appear in so many programs?
stations.fact: Cast is borrowed from metalwork: the value is poured into...

stations.name: Putting it together
bullets: A whole program reads its values, works something out and then prints the lines it was asked for.
Decide the data type each value needs before you write a single line.
Common mistake: printing the lines in a different order from the one the task asked for.
stations.challenge: Which parts of a program have to happen before anything can be printed?
stations.fact: Input, process, output is such a common pattern that it is shortened to...

final.name: Final challenge: name the data type
final.intro: Eight values are waiting on the floor below you. Tap the star and sort each one into the data type Python would store it as.

info.title: Start here: how this course works
info.text: Python is a language for writing instructions a computer follows, one line at a time. You write them in the editor on the right of a task window. Run follows your instructions and shows whatever they display in the panel underneath, labelled Program output. Check my answer is different: it marks your program against the task. So run as often as you like while you are trying things out, and check when you think it is right. You can check as many times as you like, and your best mark is the one that is kept. You work through the course in order and complete every question: the next one opens when this one is finished, because each activity teaches what the next one needs. If you are stuck, the Hint button gives you one step at a time, starting with the idea and never with the answer, and Syntax reminder lists every Python command the course has taught so far. I need help is there from the first attempt on every question - it costs you nothing, and it will tell you to ask your teacher and show them the question and your code. Errors are a normal part of programming. Everyone writing Python sees them all day, and reading the message is how you find out what to change. Work round this room through the six numbered badges in order, then tap the star for the final challenge. A badge that says Later is not open yet: finish the one you are on first. Your progress saves after every answer, so you can stop and come back to the same question.

info.title: Naming rules
info.text: A Python variable name can hold letters, digits and underscores, but it cannot start with a digit or contain a space. Capitals are used for the name of a constant, so a reader can see at a glance that the value is not meant to change.

info.title: Why it waits
info.text: input() reads one whole line, so the program only carries on once the Enter key has been pressed. Nothing else happens while it waits.

info.title: One bit each
info.text: A boolean has only two possible values, so it needs just one bit of storage - the smallest piece of data there is.

info.title: Silent rounding
info.text: int() on a float throws the decimal part away instead of rounding, so int(3.9) is 3.

info.title: Reading an error
info.text: A traceback names the line that failed. Read its last line first: that says what Python could not do.

exam.q: A pupil writes two lines to add 1 to a number that has been typed in: `n = input()` and then `print(n + 1)`. State what Python does when these two lines run, and rewrite them so that they work.
Write a program that reads a word and then a whole number, adds 1 to the number, and prints the word on one line and the new number on the next line.
Write a program that reads a number which may have a decimal point, and prints one line in the form Value is 4.0, with the number shown as a real number.

confidence: Printing lines of output in the right order
Holding values in variables and constants
Casting between text and numbers

title: Arithmetic
subtitle: Revise 360 Python course  |  Beyond the OCR J277 specification
intro: Computers were built to calculate, and Python has an operator for every kind of sum in the specification. Work through the six stations and learn which one to reach for, and what each one hands back.
objectives: know which arithmetic operator each kind of calculation needs
understand the difference between /, // and % and what each one hands back
know how to round a result, and how to draw a random number from a seed
starter: Work these out by hand, with no computer: 17 / 5, 17 // 5, 17 % 5 and 2 ** 5. Beside each answer write whether Python shows a whole number or a decimal.
keyq: How do you choose between /, // and % when the answer to a calculation has to come out as a whole number?

stations.name: The four operations
bullets: + adds, - subtracts, * multiplies and / divides.
/ always gives a float, so 10 / 2 shows as 5.0 rather than 5.
Common mistake: writing 2n for two lots of n, when Python needs 2 * n.
stations.challenge: Why does dividing one whole number by another leave a decimal point on the answer?
stations.fact: The * was chosen for multiply because early keyboards had no...

stations.name: Whole number division
bullets: // divides and throws the remainder away, giving a whole number.
% gives only the remainder, and is called the modulus.
Common mistake: using / when the answer must be whole, which leaves a .0 on the end.
stations.challenge: Which two operators turn 250 pence into a number of whole pounds and the pence left over?
stations.fact: // and % are a pair: one gives the whole part and the other gives...

stations.name: Powers and roots
bullets: ** raises a number to a power, so 5 ** 2 is 25 and 5 ** 3 is 125.
A square root is the power of 0.5, or math.sqrt() once math has been imported.
Common mistake: writing 5 ^ 2, which does something else entirely in Python.
stations.challenge: Give two different ways of working out the square root of 49.
stations.fact: Raising a number to the power 0.5 gives its...

stations.name: Rounding
bullets: round(x) gives the nearest whole number, and round(x, 2) keeps two decimal places.
abs() removes the sign, so a difference can be reported without saying which way.
Common mistake: rounding early, then carrying the rounded value into the next calculation.
stations.challenge: Why does an average almost always need rounding before it is printed?
stations.fact: Python rounds a value ending in exactly .5 towards the...

stations.name: Random numbers
bullets: import random first, then random.randint(a, b) gives a whole number from a to b, both included.
random.seed(n) makes the same sequence come out every time, so an answer can be marked.
Common mistake: calling randint again instead of storing the number you have already drawn.
stations.challenge: Why would a program ever want its random numbers to be predictable?
stations.fact: A computer works its random numbers out with a formula, so they are really...

stations.name: Putting it together
bullets: Work out the order of a calculation before you type it: brackets, powers, then * / // %, then + -.
Store a part-finished answer in a named variable to keep a long calculation readable.
Common mistake: leaving brackets out, so Python works the sum out in a different order from the one you meant.
stations.challenge: In what order does Python work through 2 + 3 * 4 ** 2?
stations.fact: BIDMAS in a maths lesson is the same rule Python uses for...

final.name: Final challenge: pick the operator
final.intro: Eight jobs are waiting on the floor below you. Tap the star and choose the operator or function each one needs.

info.title: Dividing by zero
info.text: Any program that divides by a number the user typed should check it is not zero first, or Python stops with an error.

info.title: Clock arithmetic
info.text: % is how a program wraps round: hour 25 on a 24-hour clock is 25 % 24, which is 1.

info.title: Any root at all
info.text: Every root can be written as a power, so a cube root is the power of one third and 27 ** (1/3) is 3.

info.title: Floats are close, not exact
info.text: 0.1 + 0.2 does not give exactly 0.3, because a float is stored in binary and some decimals will not fit.

info.title: The same every time
info.text: random.seed() fixes where the sequence starts, so the same seed always produces the same numbers. That is how a program that draws random numbers can still be marked.

info.title: Why order matters
info.text: Without an agreed order, 2 + 3 * 4 could mean 20 instead of 14, so every language fixes one.

exam.q: A program works out how many whole 6s go into a number, and the line reads `lots = n / 6`. State what is wrong with the result this gives, and write the line corrected.
Write a program that reads a whole number of pence and prints how many whole pounds are in it, then how many pence are left over on the next line.
Write a program that reads three whole numbers and prints their average, rounded to one decimal place.

confidence: Choosing the right arithmetic operator
Using // and % for whole-number answers
Rounding a result and seeding a random number

title: Selection
subtitle: Revise 360 Python course  |  Beyond the OCR J277 specification
intro: A program that always does the same thing is not much use. Work through the six stations and you will write the conditions that let a program choose, from a single comparison to a whole nest of them.
objectives: know how to write a condition using the comparison operators
understand how if, elif and else choose between several outcomes
know how to join two conditions together with and, or and not
starter: A program has three branches: if n > 20 it prints big, elif n > 10 it prints middle, and else it prints small. Write down what is printed when n is 30, when it is 11, and when it is 10.
keyq: Why does the order the branches are written in change what an if ... elif ... else actually does?

stations.name: Comparing values
bullets: A comparison gives a boolean back: either True or False.
The comparison operators are ==, !=, >, <, >= and <=.
Common mistake: comparing with one =, when one = stores a value and two compare them.
stations.challenge: What does a > b print when a is 5 and b is 5?
stations.fact: A value that can only be True or False is named after George Boole, so it is called a...

stations.name: if and else
bullets: if runs the indented block below it only when its condition is True.
else catches every other case, and needs no condition of its own.
Common mistake: missing the colon, or not indenting the block underneath it.
stations.challenge: Why does a rule worded as '20 or more' need >= rather than >?
stations.fact: Python uses indentation where most languages use brackets, so the layout is part of the...

stations.name: elif
bullets: elif adds another condition, which is only tested if the ones above it were False.
Python stops at the first branch that is True and skips everything below.
Common mistake: putting a wide band first, so it catches everything and the later branches never run.
stations.challenge: Why must the bands of a grade boundary list be tested in order?
stations.fact: elif is short for two words that some languages make you write out in full:...

stations.name: AND, OR and NOT
bullets: and is True only when both sides are, and or is True when at least one side is.
not flips a condition over, so not found is True whenever found is False.
Common mistake: writing n == 3 or 7, which Python reads as something quite different.
stations.challenge: How would you test in one condition whether a number is either 3 or 7?
stations.fact: Python stops reading an and as soon as one side is False, which is called...

stations.name: Decisions inside decisions
bullets: A decision can sit inside another, and the inner one is only reached if the outer was True.
Each level of nesting is indented one more step in than the one above.
Common mistake: nesting where a single and would have said the same thing far more clearly.
stations.challenge: When is a nested if clearer than one condition joined with and?
stations.fact: Deeply nested ifs are so hard to follow that programmers call the shape the...

stations.name: Putting it together
bullets: Work the boundaries out first, then write the bands in the order the rules apply.
Test on the edge of every band, because that is exactly where conditions go wrong.
Common mistake: using > where the rule says 'or more', which loses the boundary value.
stations.challenge: Which three values would you test on a program whose bands change at 30 and 50?
stations.fact: A mistake at the edge of a band is so common that it has its own name: an...

final.name: Final challenge: true or false
final.intro: Three variables hold these values: wind is 15, vis is 8 and alarm is False. Tap the star and decide whether each condition is True or False.

info.title: One = or two
info.text: A single = stores a value and == compares two. Mixing them up is one of the first bugs every programmer meets.

info.title: No switch here
info.text: Some languages have a switch statement for choosing between many options. Python does the same job with elif.

info.title: Unreachable code
info.text: If a band that catches everything is tested first, no branch below it can ever run - those lines are unreachable.

info.title: Same as the gates
info.text: and, or and not behave exactly like the AND, OR and NOT gates you draw truth tables for in topic 2.4.

info.title: Flatten it
info.text: A nested if can often be replaced by one condition joined with and, which is easier to read and easier to test.

info.title: Read the wording
info.text: 'At least', 'no more than' and 'over' all mean different things. Write the boundary value down before you code it.

exam.q: A program should print cheap when a number is 2 or less and dear when it is more. A pupil writes `if n > 2` then prints cheap, and else prints dear. Identify the logic error and write the two lines corrected.
Write a program that reads a whole number and prints small when it is 10 or less, medium when it is more than 10 but 100 or less, and large when it is more than 100.
Write a program that reads a whole number and then a word, and prints open only when the number is 3 or 7 and the word is not locked. Otherwise it prints refused.

Choosing between if, elif and else
Joining conditions with and, or and not

title: Count-controlled loops
subtitle: Revise 360 Python course  |  Beyond the OCR J277 specification
intro: When you know how many times something has to happen, a counting loop does it for you. Work through the six stations and you will learn to control a for loop and to use the number it counts with.
objectives: know how to write a for loop that repeats a block a set number of times
understand how range() decides which values the loop counter takes
know how to build a running total inside a loop, and how to put one loop inside another
starter: Write down every number printed by for i in range(2, 9, 3), then say how many lines of output there are altogether.
keyq: How do you decide what to put inside range() so that a loop counts exactly the values you want?

stations.name: Repeating a line
bullets: for i in range(4): runs the indented block below it four times.
Count-controlled iteration is used when the number of repeats is known in advance.
Common mistake: leaving the line to repeat outside the loop, so it only runs once.
stations.challenge: How would you repeat a line as many times as the user asks for?
stations.fact: Iteration is the proper name for repetition, and it is one of the three basic...

stations.name: Using the counter
bullets: The loop variable holds the count on each pass, so you can print it or calculate with it.
range(n) counts from 0, so the values are 0 up to n - 1.
Common mistake: expecting range(5) to include 5, or to start at 1.
stations.challenge: What has to change so that a loop counts from 1 up to and including n?
stations.fact: Counting from 0 is normal in programming, and it is why the first item of a list is item...

stations.name: Choosing the range
bullets: range(start, stop) counts from start up to but not including stop.
A third value is the step, so range(10, 0, -2) counts back down in twos.
Common mistake: forgetting stop is never reached, which quietly loses the last value.
stations.challenge: Which range counts through 4 to 9, with both of them included?
stations.fact: The stop value of a range is the one value the loop never...

stations.name: Running totals
bullets: A running total is set to 0 before the loop and grows inside it.
total = total + value adds this pass's value to whatever is already there.
Common mistake: setting the total back to 0 inside the loop, which loses everything counted so far.
stations.challenge: Where must a running total be set to zero, and why there?
stations.fact: A counter and a running total work the same way: one adds 1 and the other adds...

stations.name: Loops inside loops
bullets: A nested loop runs the whole inner loop on every single pass of the outer one.
Rows and columns are the usual job: the outer loop picks the row, the inner one the column.
Common mistake: indenting the inner loop's body wrongly, so all the rows run together.
stations.challenge: How many lines does a loop of 4 columns inside a loop of 3 rows print?
stations.fact: Nesting one loop inside another multiplies the work rather than...

stations.name: Putting it together
bullets: Decide what each loop counts before you write it, and name the loop variable after that.
Build the total, the count and the average from the same single pass through the data.
Common mistake: printing inside the loop when the task asks for one line at the end.
stations.challenge: Which figures can one pass through the data work out at the same time?
stations.fact: One pass that gathers several answers at once beats looping over the same data...

final.name: Final challenge: how many times?
final.intro: Eight loops are waiting on the floor below you. Tap the star and sort each one by how many times its block runs.

info.title: Three structures
info.text: Sequence, selection and iteration are the three building blocks of every program ever written.

info.title: Why i
info.text: The loop variable is traditionally i, for index, with j and k for nested loops - but a name that says what it counts is clearer.

info.title: Counting down
info.text: A negative step counts backwards, which is how a program works through a list from the end to the start.

info.title: One pass, many answers
info.text: A single loop can build a total, a count and a highest value all at once, which saves going through the data twice.

info.title: Multiplying work
info.text: Nesting multiplies: three loops of 1000 inside each other would run a thousand million times.

info.title: Which loop
info.text: If you know the number of repeats, use for. If it depends on what happens, use while - which is the next lesson.

exam.q: A program should print the numbers 1 to 10 but prints 0 to 9 instead. Its loop begins `for i in range(10)`. State which values the original `range()` counted through, and rewrite the line so the loop prints 1 to 10.
Write a program that reads how many numbers there are, then reads that many whole numbers and prints their total and their average.
Write a program that reads a whole number and prints that many lines, the first holding one * character, the second two, and so on.

Keeping a running total inside a loop
Using one loop inside another

title: Condition-controlled loops
subtitle: Revise 360 Python course  |  Beyond the OCR J277 specification
intro: Sometimes a program cannot know how many repeats it needs until it is already running. Work through the six stations and you will write condition-controlled loops that keep going until something changes.
objectives: know how to write a while loop and what makes it stop repeating
understand how a validation loop keeps asking until the value typed in is acceptable
know how a sentinel value ends a loop when the amount of data is not known in advance
starter: A program sets count = 5, then a while loop runs for as long as count > 0, and the only line inside the loop prints count. Describe what happens when this program runs, and write down the one line that is missing.
keyq: How do you decide between a for loop and a while loop before you write a single line of code?

stations.name: A loop with a condition
bullets: while repeats its block for as long as its condition stays True.
The condition is tested before every pass, so a while loop can run no times at all.
Common mistake: never changing the condition inside the loop, which leaves it running forever.
stations.challenge: What has to change inside a while loop for it ever to stop?
stations.fact: A loop whose condition never becomes False will freeze the program, and is called an...

stations.name: Asking until it is right
bullets: A validation loop reads a value, then asks again for as long as it breaks the rules.
Read once above the loop, then read again at the bottom of it.
Common mistake: leaving the second read out, so the same bad value is tested forever.
stations.challenge: Why does a validation loop need an input() in two different places?
stations.fact: A loop that keeps asking until the value is acceptable has a name of its own, and it is the heart of topic 2.3:...

stations.name: Sentinel values
bullets: A sentinel is an agreed value meaning 'no more data', such as -1 or the word end.
The loop keeps going until the sentinel arrives, however many values came before it.
Common mistake: counting the sentinel itself as one of the real values.
stations.challenge: Why must a sentinel be a value the real data can never take?
stations.fact: Sentinel means guard, because the value stands at the end of the data...

stations.name: Counting inside a while
bullets: A counter and a running total are set up before the loop and updated inside it.
The same pass can count the values and test each one against a rule.
Common mistake: updating the counter after the loop has already finished.
stations.challenge: How would you count how many of the numbers read reached 40?
stations.fact: A while loop with a counter can do anything a for loop can, but a for loop says it more...

stations.name: Choosing for or while
bullets: Use for when the number of repeats is known before the loop starts.
Use while when it depends on the data, or on what the user chooses to type.
Common mistake: a while loop with its own counter where a for loop would be shorter and safer.
stations.challenge: Which kind of loop does a program need when it cannot know how many repeats there will be?
stations.fact: Both for and while are kinds of iteration, so in the exam you must name the kind you have...

stations.name: Putting it together
bullets: Set every total and counter up before the loop, and report them after it.
One while loop can both check what comes in and gather the figures you need.
Common mistake: reporting inside the loop, which prints a line for every value read.
stations.challenge: What should a program print when the sentinel is the very first thing typed?
stations.fact: A loop that reads until a sentinel copes with no data at all, as long as the totals start at...

final.name: Final challenge: for or while?
final.intro: Eight jobs are waiting on the floor below you. Tap the star and decide whether each one needs a count-controlled for loop or a condition-controlled while loop.

info.title: Stuck forever
info.text: If a program stops responding, an infinite loop is often why: the condition it waits for can never become False.

info.title: Ask again politely
info.text: A good validation loop says what was wrong with the last answer, not just 'try again'.

info.title: Choosing a sentinel
info.text: -1 works when the real values can never be negative. For a temperature it would be a terrible choice.

info.title: Count or total
info.text: A counter always adds 1. A running total adds whatever came in. Plenty of programs need both at once.

info.title: Testing at the bottom
info.text: Some languages have a loop that tests its condition at the end, so it always runs once. Python does not, so the first read goes above the loop.

info.title: No data at all
info.text: A program given no data should still print something sensible. Start every total at zero and it will.

exam.q: A validation loop reads a whole number, then repeats for as long as it is outside 1 to 20. When 99 is typed the program prints out of range over and over. State what has been left out of the loop, and where in the loop it belongs.
Write a program that reads whole numbers until -1 is typed, then prints how many numbers were read and their total.
Write a program that keeps asking for a word until yes or no is typed, printing please answer yes or no for every other word, and then prints the word that was accepted.

confidence: Writing a while loop that stops
Writing a validation loop that asks again
Using a sentinel value to end a loop

title: String handling
subtitle: Revise 360 Python course  |  Beyond the OCR J277 specification
intro: Text is the data programs handle most, and Python has a tool for every part of it. Work through the six stations and you will measure, cut, compare and search strings.
objectives: know how to find the length of a string and the character at a given position
understand how a slice takes part of a string, and why its end position is left out
know how to change case, search inside text, and move between a character and its code
starter: The variable word holds Cavendish. Write down what each of these gives: len(word), word[0], word[0:4], word[-1] and word.upper().
keyq: Why are the characters of a string numbered from 0 rather than from 1?

stations.name: Length and position
bullets: len() gives the number of characters in a string, spaces included.
Characters are numbered from 0, so the last one sits at len() - 1.
Common mistake: asking for position len(), which is one past the end and stops the program.
stations.challenge: Which position holds the last character of a six-letter word?
stations.fact: A negative index counts from the end, so word[-1] is always the...

stations.name: Taking part of a string
bullets: A slice takes a run of characters, so word[0:3] gives the first three.
The first number is included and the second is not, exactly like range().
Common mistake: expecting word[0:3] to give four characters rather than three.
stations.challenge: Which slice gives everything except the first and last characters?
stations.fact: In a slice the first number is included and the second one is...

stations.name: Upper and lower case
bullets: upper() and lower() hand back a new string and leave the original untouched.
Comparing two strings in the same case ignores how they happened to be typed.
Common mistake: calling lower() but never storing or using what it gives back.
stations.challenge: Why does a program put two words into the same case before deciding they match?
stations.fact: Strings are compared by character code, so in Python every capital sorts before every...

stations.name: Searching inside text
bullets: in tests whether one string appears anywhere inside another.
find() gives the position it starts at, or -1 when it is not there at all.
Common mistake: treating find()'s 0 as 'not found', when 0 means the very start.
stations.challenge: How can a program tell 'not found' apart from 'found at the start'?
stations.fact: Two methods answer the commonest search questions on their own: startswith() and...

stations.name: Character codes
bullets: Every character is stored as a number, and ord() gives that number.
chr() goes the other way, turning a code back into its character.
Common mistake: adding 1 to the letter itself, when it is the code that has to be added to.
stations.challenge: How would you work out the letter that comes after a given one?
stations.fact: A is 65 and a is 97, so the gap between a capital and its small letter is always...

stations.name: Putting it together
bullets: Build a new string one character at a time inside a loop over the original.
isalpha() and isdigit() sort the letters from the digits as you go.
Common mistake: trying to change one character in place, when a string cannot be edited.
stations.challenge: How would you build a reversed copy of a word one character at a time?
stations.fact: A word that reads the same backwards as forwards is called a...

final.name: Final challenge: what does it give?
final.intro: A variable called word holds LANTERN. Tap the star and match each piece of Python to what it gives back.

info.title: Spaces count
info.text: len() counts every character, so a space, a comma and a full stop each add one to the length.

info.title: Open ends
info.text: A slice can leave a number out: word[:3] starts at the beginning and word[3:] runs to the end.

info.title: Nothing is changed
info.text: upper() does not change the original - it hands back a new string. Strings in Python cannot be edited in place.

info.title: Searching fairly

title: Subprograms
subtitle: Revise 360 Python course  |  Beyond the OCR J277 specification
intro: Long programs are built out of small named parts, each one written once and called whenever it is wanted. Work through the six stations and you will write procedures and functions, pass values into them with parameters and get answers back out with return.

stations.name: Writing a procedure

info.title: Why bother
info.text: A job written once and called from four places is tested once and fixed once. The same lines copied four times are four bugs waiting to happen.

info.title: Default values
info.text: A parameter can be given a default value in the definition, so the subprogram still runs when the caller leaves that argument out. The default is used only when no value is handed over.

info.title: Returning more
info.text: return can hand back several values at once, separated by commas, and the caller unpacks them.

info.title: Already written
info.text: len(), int() and round() are functions somebody else wrote: you call them exactly the way you call your own.

info.title: Globals are risky

info.title: Where it looks
info.text: A program looks for a file in the folder it is running in, unless you give it a fuller path.

info.title: One line at a time
info.text: Looping straight over the file object reads it a line at a time, which matters when a file is too big to fit in memory.

info.title: No undo
info.text: Write mode empties the file the instant it opens, before you have written anything at all.

info.title: Why append exists
info.text: Append mode adds to the end without touching a single line already in the file. That is what makes it the safe mode for a file that is added to over and over.

info.title: A table in disguise

info.title: Closing safely

title: Searching and sorting
subtitle: Revise 360 Python course  |  Beyond the OCR J277 specification
intro: You met these algorithms in topic 2.1 and traced them on paper. Now you will write them. Work through the six stations and every search and every sort is yours to code, not just to describe.
objectives: know how to code a linear search and a binary search, and report the position each one finds
understand how a bubble sort, an insertion sort and a merge sort each put a list in order
know how to count the comparisons an algorithm makes, in order to compare two of them
starter: The sorted list holds 3, 8, 12, 19, 24, 31, 40. Write down the value a binary search looks at first, second and third while it hunts for 40, and how many comparisons that took.
keyq: Why is a binary search so much faster than a linear search on a long list, and what does using one cost you?

stations.name: Linear search
bullets: A linear search checks each item in turn until it finds the one it wants.
It works on any list, in order or not, and reports the position or that nothing matched.
Common mistake: printing 'not found' inside the loop, once for every item that did not match.
stations.challenge: Why must 'not found' be decided after the loop has finished?
stations.fact: A linear search over a million items may need a million comparisons, which is why sorted data is...

stations.name: Binary search
bullets: A binary search looks at the middle item, then throws away the half that cannot hold the answer.
It only works on a list that is already in order.
Common mistake: not moving low or high, which leaves the loop checking the same middle forever.
stations.challenge: How much of the list can a binary search rule out with its first comparison?
stations.fact: Doubling the length of the list adds only one more comparison, so a million items need about...

stations.name: Bubble sort
bullets: A bubble sort compares each neighbouring pair and swaps them if they are the wrong way round.
Every pass pushes the largest remaining value to the end, so n items need up to n - 1 passes.
Common mistake: a swap that loses a value, because one side was overwritten before it was copied.
stations.challenge: How does a bubble sort know that it can stop early?
stations.fact: A whole pass that makes no swaps at all means the list is already in order, so the sort can...

stations.name: Insertion sort
bullets: An insertion sort takes the next item and slides it back into place among the sorted ones.
The front of the list is always in order, and it grows by one item each time round.
Common mistake: overwriting an item instead of shifting it along to make room.
stations.challenge: Which part of the list is already sorted part way through an insertion sort?
stations.fact: An insertion sort is how most people put a hand of cards in order without ever being...

stations.name: Merge sort
bullets: A merge sort splits the list in half over and over, then merges the pieces back in order.
Merging compares the front of each sorted list and takes the smaller one each time.
Common mistake: stopping when one list runs out, instead of copying the rest of the other.
stations.challenge: Why is merging two sorted lists easier than sorting one unsorted one?
stations.fact: A merge sort usually beats a bubble sort on a long list, but what it costs you is extra...

stations.name: Putting it together
bullets: Count the comparisons to compare two algorithms fairly on exactly the same data.
Write the search or the sort out yourself, since sorted() and .index() hide the very steps being counted.
Common mistake: binary searching a list that was never sorted, which quietly gives the wrong answer.
stations.challenge: Plan an experiment that shows a binary search beating a linear one.
stations.fact: Sorting costs time too, so for one single search on unsorted data the winner can still be a...

final.name: Final challenge: which algorithm?
final.intro: Eight descriptions are laid out on the floor below you. Tap the star and sort each one into the algorithm it describes.

info.title: The found flag
info.text: A flag set to False before the loop is the tidiest way to report 'not found' exactly once. The position a search finds is useful in itself: it reads the matching item out of a second list filled in the same order.

info.title: Whole middles only
info.text: mid = (low + high) // 2 uses // so the middle is a whole number: a list index can never be 3.5.

info.title: Swapping in one line
info.text: Python can swap two values in one line with a, b = b, a. Most languages need a third variable to hold one of them.

info.title: Nearly sorted
info.text: On a list that is almost in order an insertion sort is very quick, because hardly anything has to move. The same code sorts words as well as numbers, because > compares two strings by character code.

info.title: Divide and conquer
info.text: Splitting a problem into smaller copies of itself is called divide and conquer, and merge sort is the classic example.

info.title: When it matters
info.text: On a short list any sort is fast enough. The difference only shows up on large data - which is where the exam questions live.

stations.name: Putting it together
bullets: Validate each value in its own loop before the program moves on to the next one.
A program that keeps going when one line of data is wrong is more useful than one that stops.
Common mistake: validating at the end, when the first bad value has already been used.
stations.challenge: Which checks does a username need, and in which order should they run?
stations.fact: Naming a bad line and carrying on is usually better than stopping, because the run still...

final.name: Final challenge: which check?
final.intro: Eight rules are listed on the floor below you. Tap the star and sort each one into the kind of check it is.

info.title: A list of allowed values
info.text: Some values are only valid if they appear on a list the program already holds, which is a lookup check. Comparing exactly means one capital letter makes a value unknown, so decide whether to lower() both sides first.

info.title: Inclusive means both
info.text: 'From 1 to 10 inclusive' means 1 and 10 both pass. Test them: that is exactly what boundary data is for. Watch out that isdigit() calls a minus sign a non-digit, so a range allowing negatives needs that sign checked on its own.

info.title: Length, then format
info.text: Checking the length first means a format check can safely look at a particular position in the string.

info.title: Say what was wrong
info.text: A loop that only answers 'invalid' leaves the user guessing. Testing the rules one at a time lets the program name the rule that was broken, which is why these checks are usually written as if ... elif ...

info.title: Never stored plainly
info.text: Real systems never keep a password as it was typed. They store a hash of it, which cannot be read back.

info.title: Keep going
info.text: A program that skips a bad line and says how many it skipped is more useful than one that stops at the first problem.

title: SQL queries
subtitle: Revise 360 Python course  |  Beyond the OCR J277 specification
intro: A database holds far more than a program could ever keep in memory, and SQL is how you ask it a question. Work through the six stations and you will write queries against a table called games, choosing the columns you want, keeping only the rows you want and putting them in order.
objectives: know how SELECT and FROM choose the fields and the table a query reads
understand how WHERE decides which records a query hands back
know how to join conditions with AND and OR, and how to put results in order with ORDER BY
starter: A table called Tree holds the fields Name, Height and Native, and 30 records. Write down how many fields and how many records come back from SELECT Name, Height FROM Tree, and which clause you would add to cut the records down.
keyq: Which clause of a query decides which fields come back, and which clause decides which records?

stations.name: SELECT and FROM
bullets: SELECT names the fields you want, and FROM names the table they live in.
SELECT * means every field, and with no WHERE every record comes back.
Common mistake: listing the fields in the wrong order, since results come out in the order you asked for.
stations.challenge: Which part of a query decides how many records come back?
stations.fact: SQL stands for Structured Query Language, and what it is for is asking rather than...

stations.name: WHERE
bullets: WHERE filters the records, keeping only the ones whose condition is true.
Text to match goes inside quotes, and numbers do not.
Common mistake: leaving the quotes off text, so SQL looks for a field with that name instead.
stations.challenge: Which records come back from a query that has no WHERE at all?
stations.fact: WHERE looks at each record on its own and decides, for that one record, whether to...

stations.name: Comparing values
bullets: The comparisons are =, <>, >, <, >= and <=, and they work on numbers and on text.
'Longer than 45' is > 45, but '45 or longer' is >= 45.
Common mistake: using > where the question says 'or more', which loses the boundary record.
stations.challenge: Write the WHERE clause for games lasting 45 minutes or longer.
stations.fact: SQL writes 'not equal to' as <>, where the same test in Python is written...

stations.name: AND and OR
bullets: AND keeps a record only when both conditions hold; OR keeps it when either one does.
Brackets make the meaning clear when AND and OR appear in the same WHERE.
Common mistake: using AND where the question means OR, which often gives no records at all.
stations.challenge: Why would AND give nothing for 'under 20 minutes or over 60'?
stations.fact: AND narrows the records down while OR widens them out, so the one that can only ever give you fewer records is...

stations.name: Sorting results
bullets: ORDER BY sorts the results by a field, smallest or earliest first.
DESC reverses that, so the largest or latest comes first instead.
Common mistake: putting ORDER BY before WHERE, when it always comes last.
stations.challenge: Which clause lists the longest games first?
stations.fact: Ascending is the order ORDER BY uses unless you say otherwise, and the word that asks for the other direction is...

stations.name: Putting it together
bullets: The clauses always come in the order SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY.
Build a query one clause at a time and check what comes back at every step.
Common mistake: mixing up the quotes, so a word is read as a field name and the query finds nothing.
stations.challenge: Write a query for games that are not card games and last an hour or less, longest first.
stations.fact: One query can filter and sort at once, which is why that work belongs in the query and not in...

final.name: Final challenge: build the query
final.intro: The table games has the fields title, kind, players and minutes. Tap the star and put the clauses of one query into the order SQL needs them.

info.title: Asking, not telling
info.text: SQL says what you want, not how to get it. The database works the steps out for itself.

info.title: Quotes matter
info.text: WHERE kind = card looks for a field called card and fails. WHERE kind = 'card' looks for the word.

info.title: Boundaries again
info.text: 'Over 60' and '60 or more' are different queries. The off-by-one that bites in Python bites here too.

info.title: Use brackets
info.text: WHERE a AND b OR c can mean two different things, and brackets say which one you meant.

info.title: Sorting text
info.text: ORDER BY on a text field sorts alphabetically, which is how a list of names is put into order.

info.title: Why a database
info.text: A database holds far more than a program's memory, and many people can query the same table at the same time.
